title: Short Stuff: Smudging: Not just for hippies
summary: Short Stuff episode on smudging, the practice of burning sage (or other herbs) to cleanse a space or person of negative energy. Josh and Chuck cover its Indigenous North American roots (Dakota and Ho-Chunk, the latter formerly known as the Winnebago tribe), the lack of rigorous scientific study on smudging versus studies of sage extract or havan samagri incense, claimed benefits such as negative ions counteracting allergens, the decline of California white sage and responsible harvesting, cultural appropriation concerns, the four-element symbolism of smudging (abalone shell for water, herb bundle, fire, smoke for air), intention-setting and prayer per writer Molly Larkin, and disposing of ashes on bare earth. They close with a note to smudge ethically and respectfully.

segments.title: Introduction to smudging
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce smudging, the burning of sage to clear bad vibes, and its roots in Dakota and Ho-Chunk cultures. They note that the science is limited and encourage ethical, responsible practice.

segments.title: Cultural appropriation and respect
segments.summary: Chuck explains that sage's name comes from Latin salvia and raises cultural appropriation concerns about casual smudging with music in the background. He and Josh suggest researching the practice beyond social media.

segments.title: Pre-break teaser on benefits
segments.summary: Chuck warns that wellness websites may be inaccurate and previews a discussion of claimed smudging benefits after the break.

segments.title: Claimed benefits and lack of research
segments.summary: Chuck lists claimed benefits of burning sage, such as improved mood, sleep, cognition, and reduced stress, and notes the scarcity of rigorous studies. Josh points out that many studies concern havan samagri incense or oral sage extract rather than smudging, and advises caution while accepting placebo effects.

segments.title: Safety and sage conservation
segments.summary: Chuck advises against inhaling burning sage in a bong. He reports that about half of California white sage has been lost, citing urbanization, climate change, fire, drought, and poaching, and Josh adds that fire and new demand may contribute.

segments.title: Pollinators, smoke, and negative ions
segments.summary: Chuck notes carpenter bees are the main white sage pollinator and advises keeping smoke minimal, especially for people with asthma or respiratory illness. Josh says smoke releases negative ions that may counter allergens like dust, and mentions the Mayo Clinic's smudging room.

segments.title: Smudging ritual and bathing in smoke
segments.summary: Chuck suggests respecting the practice even as a placebo. Josh explains that traditional smudging involved bathing in sage smoke, and that the practice later expanded to clearing negative energy from a space.

segments.title: Four elements and intention
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck describe the elements of smudging: an abalone shell for water, the herb bundle, fire, and smoke for air. Josh cites writer and healing practitioner Molly Larkin on setting an intention through prayer, which can clear negative or invite positive energy.

segments.title: Ash disposal and sourcing sage
segments.summary: Josh says ashes should be disposed of on bare earth because they are believed to hold removed negative energy. The hosts recommend growing your own white sage or buying from local Native American-owned businesses rather than mass market retailers.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up by urging listeners to smudge ethically, responsibly, and with respect, and close the Short Stuff episode.
